subject: physics
title: Required practicals: waves
key_idea: Wave practicals use v = fλ, the standing-wave condition on a string, Snell's law and d sin θ = nλ. Change one variable at a time, repeat, and use graphs and several orders or wavelengths to reduce uncertainty.

sections.heading: Speed of sound with an oscilloscope

blocks.text: This practical measures the wavelength of sound from the phase of two traces, then finds the speed from v = fλ.

items.text: Connect a signal generator to a loudspeaker and to one channel of a two-beam oscilloscope. Connect a microphone to the other channel.
Set a frequency of about 2 kHz. Read the frequency from the generator, or find it from the trace as f = 1 / T.
Place the microphone close to the speaker. Adjust the settings until both traces are clear and the same size, in phase.
Move the microphone slowly away from the speaker. The traces move out of step and then back into step.
Measure the distance d moved through n in-phase positions. The wavelength is λ = d / n.
Calculate v = fλ. Repeat at other frequencies and take a mean.

diagram.alt: A sequencing activity. Put the steps of the speed of sound practical in the correct order.
diagram.prompt: Put these steps for finding the speed of sound in the correct order.
steps: Connect the speaker and the microphone to a two-beam oscilloscope.
Set the frequency on the signal generator.
Put the microphone next to the speaker with the traces in phase.
Move the microphone until the traces are next in phase again several times.
Measure the distance moved and divide by the number of wavelengths.
Calculate the speed using v = fλ.

items: Measuring across many wavelengths gives a smaller percentage error than measuring one.
Ensure the speaker and microphone are in line and well away from walls, to reduce reflections.
The speed of sound in air is about 340 m/s at room temperature.
Distance between successive in-phase positions is one wavelength.
v = fλ, with f from the generator or the trace.

sections.heading: Vibrating strings and light through a grating

blocks.text: Two core practicals use a standing wave on a string and an interference pattern from a laser.

items.text: Fix a string or wire over a pulley with weights hanging from one end, and a vibrator and signal generator at the other.
Change one of length, tension or mass per unit length. Keep the other two fixed.
Adjust the generator until the string vibrates in the first harmonic with one large loop.
Record the frequency at resonance. Repeat for a range of values.

items: Tension is the weight of the hanging masses: T = mg.
Plot f against 1/l (a straight line through the origin), f against √T and f against 1/√μ.
Each of these graphs should be a straight line through the origin if f₁ = (1 / 2l) √(T / μ).

blocks.text: Wavelength of light with a diffraction grating

items.text: Shine a laser at right angles to a diffraction grating, with a screen a measured distance D away.
Measure the distance from the central maximum to the first-order, second-order and further maxima.
Find θ from tan θ = (distance from centre) / D for each order.
Use d sin θ = nλ, with d = 1 / lines per metre, to find λ for each order. Take the mean.

items: Take measurements for both sides of the centre and use the mean to reduce error.
A graph of sin θ against n has gradient λ / d.
Never look along the laser beam, and use a low-power laser.
Change one variable at a time; the others stay constant.
For the grating, a graph of sin θ against n has gradient λ / d.

sections.heading: Measuring the refractive index of a solid

blocks.text: The refractive index of a transparent block can be found from Snell's law, using a ray box and the block.

items.text: Place a rectangular block on paper. Shine a narrow ray from a ray box at one face and mark the incident and emergent rays.
Remove the block, join the marks to find the path through it and draw the normal.
Measure the angle of incidence i and the angle of refraction r.
Repeat for at least five values of i.
Plot sin i against sin r. The gradient is the refractive index n.

items: n = sin i / sin r for a ray entering the block from air.
Use a narrow ray and a protractor with a fine scale to reduce uncertainty in the angles.
A plotted line gives a better value than a single measurement.
The gradient of sin i against sin r is the refractive index.
Repeat and plot a graph rather than relying on one reading.

checks.q: In the speed of sound practical, the microphone is moved from one in-phase position to the fifth next in-phase position, a distance of 1.70 m. The frequency is 1.0 kHz. Calculate the speed of sound.
checks.a: Five wavelengths span 1.70 m, so λ = 1.70 / 5 = 0.34 m. v = fλ = 1000 × 0.34 = 340 m/s.

checks.q: A laser of wavelength 633 nm falls on a grating with 600 lines per mm. Calculate the angle of the first-order maximum.
Describe how to find the refractive index of a glass block using a ray box.
checks.a: Shine a narrow ray at the block at several angles of incidence, mark the incident and emergent rays, and draw the path through the block. Measure i and r, and plot sin i against sin r. The gradient is the refractive index.

blocks.text: The diffraction grating practical needs the grating spacing and a measured angle; the spectrometer is not needed.

items: Shine light of unknown wavelength normally on a grating of known spacing d. It forms maxima at angles θ₁, θ₂, ... on each side of the straight-through beam.
Measure each angle, use d sin θ = nλ to calculate λ for each order, then take a mean.
